Recent findings suggest that at today’s Microsoft Ignite 2026 keynote, the tech giant introduced two upcoming frontier AI models built for what the company describes as “everyday” coding tasks. But there’s a bigger story: what these models might mean for Microsoft’s AI costs and its dependence on OpenAI.

Microsoft claims its MAI Code 2 model shows 96% of Claude Opus 5.5 performance at 5% of Opus 5.5’s price.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

According to recent reports, microsoft states MAI Code 2 offers comparable performance to GPT-6.1 Sol or Opus 5.5 at a fraction of the cost. Microsoft’s Code 2 Flash model is comparable to the lower-end GPT-6 Luna and Claude Haiku 5.5, also at considerably lower cost.

Industry observers note that this doesn’t mean that those of us who pay for $100/month subscriptions will suddenly get the equivalent for five bucks. Instead, these are usage-based metrics based on API usage.

It’s also vital to understand that the benchmarks are all Microsoft-provided. Performance numbers may well differ once the models undergo independent performance tests.

Industry observers note that throughout Satya Nadella’s keynote, Microsoft showed slides referencing a wide range of foundation models that are intended to work with Copilot and other Microsoft offerings. Microsoft famously has a multi-billion-dollar investment in OpenAI dating back to 2023, and has built many of its products and services around OpenAI intellectual property.

But now, Redmond is benchmarking its internally built models against Anthropic and OpenAI offerings, and also touting that it’s integrating these new models as optional choices for GitHub Copilot, Microsoft 365, and Fabric.

Also: 75% of developers I surveyed prefer Claude Code over Codex.

One thing that Nadella made clear in today’s keynote is how central AI is becoming in everything Microsoft does. Nearly all of those AI operations previously involved the firm paying some token fees back to the frontier model providers or customers doing the same thing.

But with high-performing models of its own, Microsoft may become substantially less dependent on outside model providers, especially for the incredible volume of fairly basic and routine AI requests that occur across the company’s vast product line.

If you think back over the history of agentic work models like ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork, you may recall that they originated as agentic coding tools. As customers adopted the coding harnesses in Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to off-label productivity applications, the AI companies noticed and packaged work-centric agentic tools that were more non-programmer-friendly.

Also: I let ChatGPT Work and Claude Cowork loose on my files – only one made me nervous.

According to recent reports, there’s a lot of similarity between a coding agent and a work agent, including understanding a complex environment, using tools to change things, and producing reliable results. Coding turns out to be a very good environment for developing and testing these capabilities, particularly because code output is highly measurable. Coding agents are effective training grounds for non-coding work agents.

Recent findings suggest that this becomes really interesting in today’s announcement. Along with Code 2 and Code 2 Flash, Microsoft announced MAI Work Flash, which it describes as having been derived from Code 2 Flash. Work Flash can help generate formulas in Excel, work with documents and instructions in Word, track decisions and extract useful information from Teams, and more.

In a recent development, think about the level of intelligence these tasks are demanding from the AI models. Not that much. As long as the models are good enough, they’ll be good enough.

If Microsoft can reduce its expenses and use reliable models at a much lower price, the company itself will be able to save quite a bit of money across its entire software economy, while at the same time maintaining a deeper level of vertical integration and, therefore, control.

Let’s run some hypothetical numbers. Let’s say a organization is spending $0.01 per AI request, which, with these new models, can drop down to $0.001 per request.

In a recent development, also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer very carefully first.

A company with a daily inference cost of a million dollars (a company like Microsoft, for example) could drop that daily cost to about $100,000. Add that up across a year, and the change in models could save $325 million annually.

Industry observers note that A million here, a million there. Pretty soon, you’re talking real money.

There’s no direct evidence that Microsoft is trying to produce replacement models for the frontier providers’ offerings. But it is an interesting and compelling story if we look at Microsoft developing its own engines for the software it sells.

Microsoft says the numbers it’s reporting at are using a 50% introductory discount. That’s why I measured against $0.001 per request instead of $0.0005 per request above.

Benchmark selection could be cherry-picking. The numbers are impressive. But as we all know, there are lies, damned lies, and benchmark results. I’m fairly sure Microsoft isn’t padding these numbers too much, because it benefits from the upcoming models more than even its own customers, but still. It’s an open matter.

The organization also described clearly that these upcoming models are not designed to handle the most challenging agentic and research workloads. You’re probably not going to use them to solve a decades-old mathematics challenge. But you’re very likely to use them to reformat your PowerPoint.

Sources indicate that speaking of reformatting your PowerPoint, Microsoft also emphasized that these new models did unusually well on visualization assignments. That’s a very good fit for not only UI design challenges but also graphics and slide production.

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (788 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, we all know AI can get expensive.
  • Also: Microsoft claims its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
  • Sources indicate that earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, we all know AI can get expensive. But does that expense result in real business value? That’s the trillion-dollar question Microsoft aims to answer with today’s introduction of Agent 365 Business Analytics.

Also: Microsoft claims its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

Sources indicate that earlier this year, Microsoft introduced Agent 365, its tool for tracking agents the way an HR department would normally track human employees. With Agent 365 Business Analytics, Microsoft is attempting to build an accounting system for AI labor. The system attempts to calculate the economic value of the work performed by agents compared with what the agents cost, and then provide a return on investment estimate.

If it works, this is some very cool stuff. Microsoft is trying to map labor-market economics onto AI usage data to create value estimates.

Also: Work IQ is Microsoft’s big bet on agent-first enterprise IT, and I have questions.

To do so, it uses real labor-costing information, including data from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, the O*NET database from the US Department of Labor, and its own LinkedIn Occupational Graph.

This data, along with data gathered from Agent 365, is aggregated into analysis intended to answer:.

The goal is to provide a comprehensive picture of AI spend against value produced.

Software accounting is long established and straightforward. We measure subscription fees, cost per seat, compute costs, burden costs (like floor space and other infrastructure), and more. But AI work doesn’t fit that model, making it very hard to quantify value.

Instead, Agent 365 Business Analytics measures cost both relative to human labor and in terms of technological expense. For example, it might look at a task and determine how much human effort that task would normally take, and then price that effort based on prevailing common labor rates.

According to recent reports, then, it might factor in how much of the task was actually done by a human vs. how much was contributed by an AI, along with the estimated value of the AI’s contribution. Then it mixes in the actual AI processing cost (whether in subscriptions, tokens, on-premises infrastructure, and cloud support).

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI – what’s upcoming.

Recent findings suggest that what comes out is a hybrid labor estimate that combines human contribution, human-replacement savings, AI costs, and then potentially AI savings over human costs. It sounds positively Orwellian. But the bottom line is that companies really haven’t been able to understand the AI bottom line.

Recent findings suggest that there’s a catch. All these numbers are estimates. In its blog post, Redmond specifically states, “Assisted hours are a directional estimate of work AI helped complete, not measured time saved or financial return.”.

According to recent reports, in other words, what Agent 365 Business Analytics estimates might not actually line up with real-world experience or expenses. It’s also possible that AI work might have been assigned because there was AI to do the work, not that the AI was saving organization labor costs with every token processed.

In other words, Microsoft may be able to tell you the economic value of AI-assisted work, but it can’t demonstrate definitively that the tech giant saved any real money.

Also: 5 reasons your manufacturer needs a chief AI officer in 2026.

Industry observers note that I find it particularly telling that this is from the manufacturer that makes PowerPoint. Because now, with Agent 365 Business Analytics, it’s entirely possible that you could produce economic dashboards that look really, really impressive, but are entirely irrelevant to real life.

That’s not to say the product is useless. But it does go to the idea that you will have to be quite disciplined in how you interpret the results and how much stock you put in them for decision-making. It is one source of possible truth, not the source of absolute truth.

Sources indicate that microsoft has been investing for decades to build out the core infrastructure of enterprise computing. AI isn’t any different when it comes to the company’s overall mission.

With Agent 365 and the firm’s related offerings, Microsoft wants to help you:.

According to recent reports, this means the firm doesn’t necessarily have to provide you with the AI model to help you run your enterprise. With integration with offerings from OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Google, Databricks, Snowflake, and others, the company doesn’t even have to provide the apps or SaaS capabilities.

But if it can get in there and manage your plumbing, help you control costs, and be the HR operation for your AI workforce, Microsoft could own a central piece of your business’s operations.

Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026, plus more AI workplace updates

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption.
  • During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.
  • Also: Microsoft says its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, AI-powered workspaces are tech companies’ latest focus, as the industry still struggles to perfect adoption. Microsoft has just put its offering into the ring.

During the keynote for the company’s Ignite conference on Tuesday, CEO Satya Nadella announced Copilot Workspaces, a collaborative, “multiplayer” surface for Copilot’s agentic capabilities.

Also: Microsoft says its upcoming AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5 at 5% of the cost.

The product, available in Frontier for now, is similar to OpenAI’s ChatGPT Space and several new Anthropic features, including Whiteboard and Sheets, which essentially merge the work tools you’re used to using with an agentic framework.

Sources indicate that “As the evolution of Copilot Notebooks, it’s where people and agents build on each other’s work,” Microsoft remarked. “An agent drafts a section of a document, and you review. You leave a comment, and an agent picks it up.”.

Microsoft also confirmed Autopilot, a sort of counterpoint agent to Copilot that “can watch Teams channels, follow up on emails, run recurring work, and manage a project — without waiting for a prompt,” as Microsoft described.

In a demo video during the keynote, the agent appeared to function similarly to OpenAI’s Dots, but for work — employees can tag their Autopilot “like a colleague,” Microsoft said, and assign it tasks.

Also: 4 ways Anthropic’s upcoming Claude Sheets beat using a Google Sheets connector.

Microsoft said the agent will be able to autonomously handle “meetings and follow-ups on its own,” though that claim may be best verified by teams themselves.

Speaking of trust, however, Microsoft noted that “Autopilot runs on the identity, security, and compliance foundation IT already uses,” and that “each Autopilot has its own Microsoft Entra Agent ID and a named manager,” meaning IT can block it as needed.

Recent findings suggest that “Its sign-ins and actions are logged under its own name, so security teams have a clear audit trail. Powered by Work IQ, it understands how your organization works within existing permissions,” Microsoft said.

Recent findings suggest that the company added that employees will soon “be able to bring their personal Autopilot into Workspaces” as well. The feature is also available in Frontier.

Recent findings suggest that nadella also announced a few other productivity features, including a “command center” called Today that spans email, calendar, meetings, tasks, and threads in Teams. Presently in private preview in Outlook and the Copilot app, it includes a personalized briefing and a feed of priorities that updates throughout the day.

“The draft is written and ready for you to edit; the schedule change is already proposed; and the forgotten follow-up is waiting for you to send it, complete with context so you can catch up swiftly,” Microsoft remarked of the feature, which sounds like an agentic briefing-cum-morning-assistant.

Also: Nearly 70% of workers use AI regularly now – but many get no time to upskill.

Microsoft also revealed that Home, now generally available, unifies Chat and Cowork into a singular starting point. That’s similar to Anthropic’s recent consolidation of its chat and agentic Cowork offerings, demonstrating an overall trend toward simplification in workplace AI.

While more companies are finally starting to see a return on their AI investment, agents are still expensive and can quickly rack up costs when unsupervised.

Microsoft announced a few tools to track this at Ignite: Agent 365 Business Analytics and Agent 365 Cost Management.

Also: Microsoft wants to put a dollar value on AI’s work – but can you trust the math?

Agent 365, which Microsoft declared last year, is the organization’s observability platform. Microsoft said Business Analytics, in Frontier Public today, provides insights on what a company is spending on AI and why, and where it’s paying off, as well as forecasts future costs. In a demo during the keynote, Microsoft highlighted how admins can see when specific agents’ costs have spiked recently and what (human) employee to notify as a result.

Industry observers note that “It starts with a fresh way to measure your investment: in work completed, not simply tokens,” Microsoft noted. “It analyzes the tasks, how long that work typically takes a person, and the share Cowork performed, providing a sophisticated view of the hours your intelligence supports and what the work is worth.”.

Cost Management lets IT see where teams are using AI down to the model.

“Leaders can set spending policies, limits, and proactive alerts and control which models are available,” Microsoft remarked. Anthropic released a similar tool last month, though it was focused more on making seats as efficient as possible on Teams and Enterprise plans.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Even in 2026, the age of Bluetooth 7 and wireless charging, some things still need to be connected the old-fashioned way, via cables. USB-C didn’t simplify everything the way we hoped, so there are still tons of cable types to choose from.

Also: Why your USB-C cables look alike, but work differently – and how to tell them apart.

Regardless of how far wireless charging has come in recent years, I still rely on plenty of cables, and have done my best to find the top options out there. No matter what cable need you have, from charging laptops to hooking up storage, one of my favorites should have you covered. I’ve also thrown in what I think are non-negotiable accessories.

This is a cable that’s literally traveled thousands of miles with me. It’s small, it’s tough, it’s a complete 4-in-1 solution, and it handles ultra-fast charging up to 240W, along with Apple’s fast charging of up to 27W.

Also: The top-selling cords, cables, and chargers readers bought this year (including a cheap favorite).

This cable transforms into the following configurations:.

I love this cable, but the connectors are a bit on the chunky side and can have problems working with phones that are in thick, ruggedized cases.

I’ve tried a lot of “armored” cables that in reality, are anything but. The Galvanox pet-proof USB-C cable, however, has passed every test I’ve pitted it against — from running it over with an office chair to trying to cut it with a knife (I drew the line at biting it).

Also: 5 USB cables and dongles that can fry hardware and steal your data – or worse.

Industry observers note that the cable looks like a shower hose, and not only does this sheathing prevent it from being chewed, but makes it highly abrasion-resistant, tangle-proof, and resistant to damage from bending. In fact, these Galvanox cables have been tested to withstand a minimum of 20,000 bends.

The connectors have also been armored, with all the easily chewable polymer replaced with hard, tasteless alloy.

There are a few companies making short USB-C cables designed to fit onto a keyring, but many of the ones I tested were pricey. So I looked to see if there was a budget option, and that’s when I came across the Vafoton PD 240W short USB-C cable.

Also: Our 3 favorite Android Auto cables (and why you might want to switch to wired).

The cable measures 5.1 inches unfolded, is coated in a soft yet durable TPU, and packs away into the keychain adapter neatly. Is this too short? Not for most applications I use it for, but sometimes I did have to put my iPhone into some strange orientations to make it work.

In a recent development, and while it might be small, it’s very capable. It can carry up to 240W of power, data at 40Gbps, and video at 8K 60Hz, and is even compatible with Thunderbolt 4 standards.

The cable is much thicker than a regular cable. / Adrian Kingsley-Hughes/ZDNET.

I recently came back from a month of traveling in Europe, and I realized I needed to up my charging cable game in 2026. I needed one cable that could handle my iPhone, AirPods, and Apple Watch.

Review: This USB-C cable has a tiny screen – and that’s precisely why you need it.

After a few cables that turned out to be a disappointment — some were dead-on-arrival, and the others died after a few days of use — I came across the ChubbyCable Tri-Flex 3-in-1 cable, and this cable is just what I needed.

According to recent reports, the ChubbyCable is built like a tank. It’s 4.1 feet long and made of a soft, tangle-free, siliconized material that feels more like a high-end audio cable. There are two USB-C ends, one that supports 100W charging and data transfer at 480 Mbps, and another that can handle 12.5W fast charging. There’s also a 2.5W Apple Watch charging puck, which is also compatible with AirPods cases that support wireless charging.

According to recent reports, want a cable that can pack itself away tidily when not in use? This is the cable for you! The Statik MagStack Pro uses the magic power of magnets to curl itself away tidily when not in use. You can make massive curls or small curls, the choice is yours.

Review: This $14 retractable USB-C cable is my secret to surviving long car rides with my kids.

On top of its trick of keeping itself tidy, it can carry up to 100W of power, the connectors are robust and have very good strain relief, and it’s nylon braided, so it resists snagging.

Just note that the cable’s maximum speed is 480MB/s, so avoid using it to connect to high-speed storage drives.

This is my go-to cable any time I need to connect a device to a Thunderbolt 4 device. It’s a 3.3-foot/1 meter cable that can handle 240W power, up to 40 Gbps data, and 8K video.

It also features a thermoplastic elastomer (TPE) jacket for added flexibility and durability, for under $10.

We’re so used to using USB-C for charging that we forget it’s also a fully featured data port, and hackers can use people’s desperation to find a charger for their phone or laptop to their advantage.

Also: I tested my USB-C cables with this free Mac app – some weren’t what they claimed.

While people who only ever charge at home, the office, or car don’t need a data-blocking cable, those who regularly charge using communal points at airports, trains, buses, and random charging kiosks will benefit from protection against attacks known as Juice jacking.

These Plugable cables all feature an E-Marker chip and allow charging up to 240W (48V/5A), but because they don’t have any data lines, all attempts at communication between the charger and the device being charged are blocked.

According to recent reports, chargerLAB Power-Z AK001 display showing voltage, amperage, and power. / Adrian Kingsley-Hughes/ZDNET.

This is five-foot/1.5-meter-long USB-C cable is capable of carrying 240W of power with a built-in USB power meter.

Also: My 7 essential laptop-bag items after decades of working remotely.

It’s totally user-friendly — you just plug it in at both ends, and the display instantly lights up, providing all the crucial statistics about the power flowing through the cable: voltage, amps, and watts.

The display even has an arrow showing the direction that the power is flowing in! This is a great touch because I’ve encountered power meters that have confused me as to what’s charging what — especially where power banks are concerned.

This might be one of the best USB-C accessories I’ve ever purchased. Although simple and straightforward, it has protected my USB-C ports from damage numerous times and prevented laptops from being pulled to the floor by people (usually me) tripping over the charging cable.

In a recent development, it’s a magnetic breakaway USB-C connector similar to Apple’s MagSafe connector, compatible with all your devices, from smartphones and tablets to power banks, docks, and laptops. The best thing is that it doesn’t slow down data transfer or charging.

Also: 10 cheap car gadgets worth every penny (we’ve tested them all).

The magnetic breakaway USB-C connector consists of two parts: the first part is the USB-C port that plugs into the device you want to protect — be that a laptop, smartphone, charger, power bank, or other device — and the other part goes on the end of the cable you’re going to use.

Recent findings suggest that super-strong neodymium magnets keep the two parts together when in use until there’s a pull on the connector, and then the two parts come apart. The magnets are very strong and pull the two parts together with a decisive snap. It’s a simple idea yet brilliantly designed.

Recent findings suggest that got a random cable laying about and need to know what it’s capable of? For this job, the right tool is the Treedix multifunction USB cable tester. This pocket-sized gadget can tell you everything you need to know about a cable (probably more than you need to), and it does it swiftly and reliably.

Sources indicate that the USB cable tester is a small box featuring an array of ports. There are USB-C and USB-A output ports and corresponding USB-C, Lightning, miniUSB, and microUSB 2.0 and microUSB 3.0 input ports for testing cables.

Also: Your headphones’ USB-C port has 4 hidden features – but you need the right cable.

The unit can handle a multitude of tests, from basic functions showing whether the cable can handle data and power transmission, along with that protocols, a printout of active lines in the cable, a resistance test, and an eMarker chip test.

If the cable being tested is equipped with an eMarker chip, you will also get information about the maximum current and voltage the cable can carry, the data transfer rate, the type of cable, and even the length of the cable.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that during the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company.
  • Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5.
  • In a recent development, MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that during the keynote at its Ignite conference on Tuesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella announced several new models from Microsoft AI (MAI), its lab within the company. But new model releases are almost a dime a dozen these days, and accelerating fast — what really stood out was how Microsoft will let its customers access those models.

Also: Microsoft says its new AI coding model rivals Claude Opus 5.5.

In a recent development, MAI said it would allow its customers to customize its frontier models with their own data and run them securely in Azure through an initiative called Licensed Weights. It’s essentially a selective approach to open-weight AI: more so than proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic, but not fully downloadable on Hugging Face like Mistral’s Le Chonk. Interested companies will need to go through their Microsoft account reps to get started.

According to recent reports, “You control who can access it. Your data and adaptations stay entirely yours. And we’ll work with you through Frontier Company to deliver the custom model and embed it in your own products and agents,” Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of MAI, stated during the keynote.

The approach should stand out to businesses looking for affordable AI that lets them retain control over their IP. Microsoft said it would only use customers’ information to train its models if they agreed.

“No one wants to pour their IQ into someone else’s model,” Suleyman said during the keynote, a nod to an argument Palantir CEO Alex Karp has made repeatedly.

The dominant, if simplified, narrative in AI has been that proprietary, expensive models boast peak capabilities but aren’t customizable, while open, cheaper models are customizable but less capable. Microsoft’s AI models don’t necessarily compete with OpenAI and Anthropic yet, but the organization has legacy sway with countless businesses. By offering a customizable AI option, it could strike a balance among major tech companies.

Western labs, including Thinking Machines and Mistral, are releasing more competitive open-weight models, but Anthropic and OpenAI still have the overwhelming majority of the enterprise AI market. Though Licensed Weights isn’t an open-weight family of models, it does diversify the open-versus-closed debate a bit and differentiate Microsoft’s offering from OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s. It’s also a smart pairing with Microsoft’s goal to balance price and performance, if businesses find it impressive enough.

Also: Microsoft unveiled Copilot Workspaces at Ignite 2026.

“Averaged over four widely used benchmarks that target the everyday enterprise coding tasks we see in GitHub Copilot, MAI Code 2 gives you 98% of the performance of GPT 6.1 Sol at just 40% of the cost, and against Opus 5.5 it’s an incredible 5% of that cost,” Suleyman noted of the new coding model the firm announced at Ignite.

Sources indicate that the company also released its fresh image editing model, MAI Image 2.7, on Tuesday, which now leads the category on Artificial Analysis while beating Nano Banana Pro and several GPT image models on price and quality. With Licensed Weights, Microsoft has positioned itself for organizations seeking a reliable blend of ROI tools, customization, security controls, and capability.

Ubuntu 27.04, Tenacious T-Rex, is set for an April 22, 2027 release. Although that seems a long way off, it’s sooner than you think. As is implied by the release number, 27.04 is not an LTS release, so it only receives support for nine months (until January 2028). The good news is that you can migrate from 27.04 to 27.10, and then to the LTS release, 28.04. The entire upgrade path ensures that you don’t have to miss a single release.

In a recent development, but what’s coming in Ubuntu 27.04? Given that it’s an interim release, you’re probably assuming that there’ll be nothing exciting to be found. Although there won’t be any game-changing additions, there will be plenty of refinements and bug fixes.

Also: I’ve used Ubuntu for 22 years – and 26.10 might be its best release yet.

It has been revealed that I’ve been using the daily release of Ubuntu 27.04 for a bit. Let’s take a look at what is currently expected in Tenacious T-Rex.

This is probably the biggest addition to the next release of Ubuntu. And although you won’t find any major changes in GNOME, there are some crucial ones. First off, there will be editable quick settings, which allow for customizing, adding, removing, and rearranging toggles and widgets. GNOME 52 will also enjoy a revamped calendar popover, which streamlines the feature to focus primarily on events, time, and weather.

It has been revealed that also: Over Ubuntu? Fedora is the Linux distro I’d hop to next – here’s why.

There will also be several improvements to window management, such as a spatial overview and a mosaic/tiling system for auto-resizing and organizing windows, a refined full-screen Alt+Tab app switcher, which will be capable of grouping older windows by application while showing newer ones individually, and finally, the ability to remember window sizing, placement, and workspace.

Sources indicate that desktop search is also getting a bit of polish by way of a redesigned popover and an improved results overlay that includes file previews, multiple actions, and search filters. And, as usual, there will be plenty of bug fixes and performance enhancements. The bump in speed is noticeable, too, in my testing.

Ubuntu 27.04 will ship with the Linux 7.6 kernel, which includes better VRAM management for gaming and expanded support for modern hardware, such as early enablement for AMD Zen 6, stable support for Intel Xe3P, mainline boot capabilities for Apple M3 Pro/Max/Ultra, and initial support for the 2026 Steam Controller.

There will also be performance gains for both the Btrfs and Ext4 file systems, which (along with the improvements in GNOME 52) will make Ubuntu 27.04 one of the best-performing releases in some time.

Also: This lightweight Linux distro revives old PCs destined for the junk pile – and it’s beautiful.

Once installed, you can use it as expected.

As of right now, that’s all we know about Tenacious T-Rex.

I will say this: I’ve come to count on Ubuntu’s latest releases to be an improvement over the previous iterations, and from what I’ve seen so far in my testing, 27.04 will not disappoint. It may not knock you back to prehistoric times, but Tenacious T-Rex will wow you with its performance and polished looks.

Some of the most popular Android smartwatches just got a battery-saving enhancement. Google released an updated version of Google Play Services on Tuesday that can help extend the battery life of a Wear OS smartwatch.

The v26.45 upgrade concerns location tracking during outdoor workouts. Wear OS smartwatch customers can now use their phone’s Global Navigation Satellite System to track their location during an outdoor workout, which can conserve battery life by outsourcing the smartwatch’s energy to the smartphone when it isn’t in Battery Saver mode.

Also: Pixel Watch 4 vs. Watch 5: Is Google’s upcoming model worth it?

It has been revealed that constantly communicating with satellites during an outdoor workout can be a battery drain, and every minute of battery life counts when you use your smartwatch for communication, workout tracking, and health monitoring. GPS services, a bright, always-on display, and continuous health sensors like SpO2 can squeeze the most juice out of your smartwatch.

According to recent reports, wear OS software is used by many of the most popular smartwatch brands, including Google, Samsung, and OnePlus. Both the Google Pixel Watch and Samsung Galaxy Watch’s largest batteries last approximately 40 hours. That’s nearly two days of use from two top Android smartwatches, but you’d be surprised how quickly it can drain.

Also: Galaxy Watch 9 review: Health data overload, but built for the future.

The patch improves battery life without consumers having to take any action or change any settings — the Google Play Services version 26.45 works quietly under the hood.

Recent findings suggest that that’s not the only Google Play Services update that Wear OS smartwatch people can take advantage of. Another recent update lets users view on their phone a larger preview of any watch face they want to install on their smartwatch.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1270 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Zdnet ↗ Open Full Page

How I use Meta Muse safely to stretch my AI budget – and what I never let it do

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1270 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Zdnet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Here’s the thing about Meta Muse: it’s considerably better than you might expect for a free AI agent.
  • It has been revealed that because it’s free, and because it’s actually really pretty good, I tend to use Muse fairly often.
  • Also: Muse booked an Airbnb without permission – and that’s not all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s the thing about Meta Muse: it’s considerably better than you might expect for a free AI agent. It’s also sketchy as all heck. That’s why I use Muse only for public information research, without giving it access to my accounts, passwords, or computer.

It has been revealed that because it’s free, and because it’s actually really pretty good, I tend to use Muse fairly often. However, because it’s sketchy as heck, I take precautions. In this article, I’ll show you what is safe to use and how to protect yourself.

Also: Muse booked an Airbnb without permission – and that’s not all.

I’ll walk you through my best-practice recommendations, which also include restricting prompts so they contain nothing that needs to be kept private. Meta is Facebook’s parent company. Let’s face it, Facebook is not a paragon of identity protection and privacy. In fact, Facebook’s primary business is turning you into an asset production machine for it to mine and monetize. Make no mistake about it: Muse expands on that considerably.

In September, I took a first hands-on look at Muse. There were five worrisome themes, all in terms of privacy and data usage:.

Also: Meta Muse is the worst AI agent for privacy.

CNET has a piece that concurs with my observations, calling Muse “a potential security nightmare.” It documented a number of cases where, despite permissions being turned off, researchers claim Muse harvested private data. I haven’t seen this behavior in my testing, but it is a major part of why I’m very careful with how I use it.

Industry observers note that so while I use Muse regularly, I never give it any personal details. I don’t let it have any access to my computer or my computer’s microphone. I never give it an assignment that requires computer use or access to any of my accounts. I don’t set up any connectors, including to my Mac apps like Notepad or Reminders.

And I most definitely do not give it access to Chrome, let it record my screen, or give it access to my payment methods through my Stripe account or Shop Pay.

It has been revealed that in addition to these obvious “what not to do” items, I also don’t use Muse interactively as a chatbot. I don’t converse with Muse. During chats, you are likely to reveal snippets of personal information. We do not want Meta to have any of that personal information. For any of the standard chatbot-type activities, I use a more trustworthy tool.

To make sure your settings are safe, read my article where I go through how I set up Muse for my use.

Put simply, Muse’s free agentic capabilities are pretty good. As an AI researcher, I need to use it just because it’s out there and it’s popular. I test these things as part of my job. But I would use it anyway because it has a fairly unique value proposition.

It has been revealed that as a basic AI tool, it’s as good as anything we had in 2025. In terms of late 2026 technology, I’d put it on a par with ChatGPT Terra or Luna, or Claude Sonnet or Haiku. Muse is definitely not at the flagship model level like ChatGPT Sol or Claude Opus, but it’s not bad.

It has been revealed that muse’s value prop has to do with how much agentic work it’s willing to do for free. All the frontier model providers meter their agentic capabilities in one way or another. For applications using the models, the AI companies sell API access by tokens. For desktop work, you can buy subscriptions, typically at $20, $100, and $200 per month.

In a recent development, for those monthly subscription fees, you get a certain amount of usage: less on the lower tiers, more if you’re a bigger spender. I have the $20-per-month ChatGPT Plus proposal, which gets me a small amount of programming and a moderate amount of agentic work a month.

I have the $100-per-month Claude Max plan, which usually gets me through a month of fairly heavy vibe coding, but I do use up my weekly allocation from time to time.

Recent findings suggest that I am constantly aware of how I am consuming my allocated usage. I don’t really want to pay more than I already am. So I try to spend my usage allocation where it will have the most impact.

Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent for free now.

According to recent reports, muse gives me an agentic tool with free usage allocation. I can give Muse non-mission-critical assignments and not worry about whether or not I’ll run out of usage. If I do, I do. I’m not using it as part of my day-to-day projects.

In a recent development, that’s Muse’s value. You can give it work that requires agentic capabilities, but limit it to assignments that are not worth upgrading one of your other paid subscriptions for.

Industry observers note that I use Muse exclusively for agentic search and analysis. I give it assignments that require a chain of web searches for information-gathering purposes. Those searches generate data that needs analysis and intelligence as the chain is processed, which then results in a report or recommendation. It’s really quite good at that.

The way I’m doing it with agentic assignments is that I’m substantially less interactive with the tool. I give it a homework assignment. Essentially, I let it go off and do that homework for me. Here are some examples of what I’ve sent it off to research.

In a recent development, all of these assignments (I’ve done a total of 46 so far) require multiple web searches and aggregation into a summary or detailed report. These are all ideal projects for an agentic researcher. Muse does the job well.

According to recent reports, one issue is that even these “incognito” searches do give away information Facebook might use. For example, they could show Meta the kinds of games I like, the fact that I want to watch demonstrates on PBS, that we had a fruit fly problem for a week, and more.

Also: How I safely run my OpenClaw AI agent 24/7 on a Mac.

My interest profile is probably a matter of public record. Heck, if you’ve been reading my articles for any time at all, you know what I’m interested in. And you know that I’m a bit of a geek. So I don’t mind the risk that Facebook will pick up on this.

But I don’t want Meta to have access to my accounts, my passwords, my computer, or any files that are personal or client-related or contain any identifying information that could lead to serious privacy or identity theft problems.

My best-practice recommendation is to lock down all of Muse’s permissions and only feed it assignments that contain interest clues that, if released publicly, wouldn’t reveal anything that you would mind having revealed.

If you do that, you can have a free agentic researcher available to you for lower-priority work. Just keep in mind that this free ride might not last. Meta does have paid aims at the same pricing tiers as the other AI providers. That said, its free access is unusually generous. I’m sure there will come a time when Meta charges, at least for those of us who don’t give it enough data to feed its prodigious data-gathering appetite.

According to recent reports, would you rather limit Meta Muse’s access or pay for another AI subscription? Let us know in the comments below.

Twenty percent of holiday shoppers are using AI agents as their first stop for research and advice, but they are not ready to have agents make purchases, according to the latest Salesforce research.

Also: What to know about early Black Friday sales.

Salesforce surveyed more than 2,500 shoppers in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia and found that 74% of shoppers trust recommendations from AI agents. Salesforce research forecasts AI-driven shopping recommendations to drive $75.8 billion in Cyber Week spending, up 13% from 2025.

Also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer.

Brands are also being noticed by AI agents, with 30% of shoppers saying they were first introduced to a new brand via AI. And most importantly, 1 in 10 (11%) shoppers would avoid a brand if an AI agent told them to.

Here are some of the key findings from the 2026 holiday shopping research.

Retailers that use AI shopping agents are seeing bigger orders and more loyal customers. The survey found that shoppers who use AI agent referrals are twice as likely to make a purchase. In addition, 39% of shoppers have used AI agents on an e-commerce site, and 80% had a positive experience, while 75% felt more loyal to the brand as a result of the AI agent experience.

Shoppers who use AI agents spend 8% more than the average buyer and purchase 23% more items per order. Brands that use AI agents are seeing seven times faster sales growth than brands without them.

Sources indicate that 1 in 3 consumers has used an AI agent, including the widely adopted Meta Muse, now used by 12% of all consumers. Grok Bot is also in high demand.

It has been revealed that the survey found that 28% of consumers give their agents multiple tasks per day. The most common use of AI agents is price comparisons, product reviews, and brainstorming for gift items. Brand discovery is a major benefit of AI agent use cases.

Sources indicate that agents as advisors are growing, but agents are not buying products yet, with only 19% of personal agent people using logic to check out. Only 9% of consumers allow their personal AI agents to have unrestricted access to their financial details, and 36% have set up a separate credit card for their AI agents.

Also: ZDNET’s favorite tech devices for 2026.

According to recent reports, the majority of consumers (73%) are not comfortable giving personal AI agents their payment information, and 49% are not interested in agents making purchases on their behalf. Consumers do not want to share their purchase history or personal data that could potentially lead to unwanted charges. Shoppers will abandon an AI agent after 2-3 mistakes. If an AI agent makes a bad recommendation, 1 in 3 consumers will blame the AI.

Retailers must adopt AI shopping agents in order to compete. Retailers must be able to service and respond to shopper agents. The ability to detect intent, buying signals, sources of dissatisfaction, and other consumer-related buying patterns at machine scale (significantly faster and higher volume than human scale) will require retailers to invest in AI agentic engagement capabilities.

Also: 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well.

Today, AI agents advise consumers on their holiday shopping journeys, but in the very near future, they will autonomously make purchasing decisions with little to no involvement from their human counterparts. The future of shopping will be more autonomous, highly personalized, and nearly frictionless. Brands that invest in agentic AI will garner the most loyalty and future business.

According to recent reports, just months after its release, Google is making its Spark agent free and officially renaming its capabilities “Tasks.” You can now toggle to it from the standard Gemini Chat setting. Reports show the rebrand started gradually in mid-October.

According to recent reports, also: Ready for a Siri AI agent? Apple under pressure to upgrade its assistant faster.

OpenAI offers its Dots agents as part of its $100 per month ChatGPT Pro tier, and Anthropic’s Claude Duet is available with paid intends, which start at $20 per month. That makes Tasks and Meta Muse — the latter was called the “worst AI agent for privacy” by ZDNET’s David Gewirtz — Substantial Tech’s most affordable personal agents on the market, though you’ll have to pay for more than five hours of access at a time.

Sources indicate that if Tasks sounds familiar, it should: The company already has a product called Google Tasks, which lets you turn emails into a checkable to-do list on the side of your inbox, among other places like Chat and Docs. This is the agentic version, obviously.

Recent findings suggest that gewirtz, ZDNET’s AI tester-in-residence, wasn’t blown away by then-Spark when he tried it last month, but had reason to believe in its eventual improvement. It’s unclear whether Tasks is meaningfully different from Spark, aside from being out of beta.

Abilities aside, what sets Tasks apart here is cost. Dots and Duet haven’t exactly impressed thus far, so free alternatives don’t have a high bar to reach yet.

Also: I tested OpenAI Dot and Anthropic Duet for weeks.

During Gewirtz’s test, when the agent was part of his $20 per month Google AI Pro plan, he used only 20% of the total five hours of usage on “four fairly substantial tests.” Without an AI plan, Gemini’s context window is 32k tokens.

In a recent development, at launch in September, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg mentioned Muse is “free to use for up to 100M tokens per week,” though Meta’s help center is not so explicit. As with most agentic products, more frequent people may want to buy more access, but more casual users now have two options to compare.

In a recent development, AI companies are vying to hook customers with their various personal agents, and price and privacy are major factors to consider. Being free with limits, Muse and Tasks are perhaps geared toward a more apprehensive user who wants to try an agent, but isn’t giving it countless tasks to take on all day. Given Muse’s reputation, some may find Tasks a bit less aggressive or risky.

Also: Don’t use Muse? How Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages.

As with other agents, Tasks, which runs on its newest Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, can handle a variety of jobs for you, from grocery shopping to booking appointments and analyzing your heating bill. Agents like these are designed for a chronically overwhelmed society trained by a reliance on tech to seek convenience and productivity in nearly every aspect of life.

Sources indicate that the feature is free in the US, Canada, Korea, Japan, Australia, and India. US users can also start tasks by emailing or texting Gemini, and can have the agent call businesses for them (except in Indiana, Louisiana, Minnesota, Montana, and Nebraska).

The change from Spark to Tasks comes just a day after Google retired Gems (which let you tailor Gemini to specific tasks), and converted existing Gems into Skills. The new landing page for Tasks emphasizes personal finance and cost-cutting as a use case, positioning itself alongside personal finance features from Anthropic and OpenAI.

Recent findings suggest that “Put Gemini on the hunt for ways to save. Identify recurring expenses you no longer need, get alerts for your most-desired deals, and more,” the page reads.

AI agents remain a privacy and security risk, because of their ability to autonomously and proactively handle tasks like placing orders (which you can set spending caps for) and reviewing files.

Sources indicate that also: Want to try ChatGPT Wallet? Read OpenAI’s liability disclaimer.

“You can adjust task settings, disconnect Google and third-party apps, or delete chat history anytime,’ Google’s blog on the release stated. Google’s upcoming Memory summary feature for Gemini lets owners view and edit the personal info the chatbot has on them.

You may not know Tom Hovey, but I can practically guarantee you’ve seen his work. That’s because, in addition to many other cool projects, Tom’s also the artist behind those illustrated graphics of everyone’s bakes on The Great British Baking Show. His unique style has been all over that show, and my TV screen, for many years.

In a recent development, I found Tom’s work recently on Threads, when he went massively viral after debunking the idea that all those food drawings are AI with a video to prove how he does it. He’s been working with digital tools for a decade, he noted, “but never ever AI.”.

Industry observers note that I asked Tom to share his homescreen with us to see how he might use his phone for his work, and also to see if I might learn any good GBBS spoilers. (Alas, none.) Here it is, plus some info on the apps he uses and why:.

In a recent development, the wallpaper: A sunrise photo of the Swan River, where I run most mornings in Perth Western Australia. We moved here permanently 6 months ago.

The apps: Apple Podcasts, Brick, Sonos, Strava, SoundCloud, Photos, Google, Google Maps, iNaturalist, Google Calendar, Chrome, NYT Games, Gmail, WhatsApp, Spotify, Discord.

Like many people I’m addicted to my phone, so bricking my phone when I get home from the studio has been amazing. I’m obsessed with running, so Strava and Runna are used every day for training and logging my runs but also hyping up my running pals.

Six apps for my kids’ primary school is too many apps.

I have weather apps but it’s kinda unnecessary now we live in Australia, because it’s either hot or really hot!

According to recent reports, iNaturalist is my newest app and I love it. It’s for documenting nature — flora and fauna. As I’m in a upcoming country, I’m enjoying discovering all the native flowers and plants I find on runs. I’ve also recently done some trial runs in Perth Hills, where I’ve run into tons of wild kangaroos and snakes. So fun! My kids also love bugs and birds, so learning all about them is cool. Also when you add your photos of nature, it geotags them and sends the details to some scientists who can understand the areas you are documenting.

Taiwan’s chipmaking giant TSMC to invest $1B in Anthropic, OpenAI

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (392 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI.
  • Sources indicate that the chipmaker’s board approved aims to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters.
  • But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that top chip manufacturer TSMC is ready to invest $1 billion in Anthropic and OpenAI. That would give the Taiwanese chipmaker direct stakes in leading AI developers, even as its own contract chipmaking business has profited enormously from the AI data center buildout.

Sources indicate that the chipmaker’s board approved aims to invest up to $500 million in OpenAI preferred stock reserved for large investors and another $500 million to purchase Anthropic common shares at the latter’s expected IPO price, according to Reuters. Such an investment may give markets “a shot of confidence as the artificial-intelligence trade highlights signs of strain,” The Wall Street Journal reported.

But analysts also warned that such circular financing among investors, suppliers, and customers has made it difficult to evaluate real market demand for AI-related hardware and services, according to the Journal.

Recent findings suggest that TSMC’s chip fabrication plants physically produce the vast majority of Nvidia’s chips designed for AI data center workloads and make most of Apple’s custom chips used in iPhones, Mac laptops and desktops, plus Apple’s planned AI computing server. Most of these fabs are located in Taiwan, but TSMC also operates fabs in Japan and China, and it has an expanding US manufacturing cluster in Arizona. It is also building a new fab in Germany.

Sources indicate that meanwhile, Anthropic and OpenAI are both purchasing huge quantities of AI hardware manufactured by TSMC for their data center projects. So TSMC’s revealed investment certainly seems to fit into the broader trend of circular financing that has become common during the AI boom, even as tech stocks have gyrated recently as investors have grown increasingly jittery.

Still, TSMC has plenty of money to spare on such a bet. Ongoing demand for AI-related chips has enabled the Taiwanese chipmaker to report six consecutive quarters of record profit, with the latest example being the company earning more than $23 billion in profit during the July through September 2026 quarter, according to Reuters.

TSMC’s planned investment in Anthropic and OpenAI also pales in comparison with circular financing deals from major US tech companies. The most notable example is Nvidia, which has invested $30 billion in OpenAI and $10 billion in Anthropic so far, in addition to putting tens of billions of dollars into many other AI and robotics companies.

5 upcoming Apple Health features you should try in iOS 27.3 – if your phone qualifies

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that apple is kicking off a newly introduced and improved Health app next month with the release of iOS 27.3.
  • Also: Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll.
  • Here are five helpful new features built into the app, along with what you’ll need to access them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that apple is kicking off a newly introduced and improved Health app next month with the release of iOS 27.3. Instead of just recording and displaying your health-related stats, the app will tap into Apple Intelligence to analyze the data and dispense advice on how to improve your health and fitness. But that reliance on AI means you’ll need the right type of iPhone to enjoy all the benefits.

Also: Apple could build its AI health chatbot from this study – how to enroll.

Here are five helpful new features built into the app, along with what you’ll need to access them.

First up, the app will offer suggestions based on data from different sources. For example, it might advise you to go for a walk at a nearby park if it detects that you’re not getting enough exercise. It may show you articles and videos about sleep if it finds that you’re not well-rested. It could also highlight possible conditions based on your lab and test results. You can easily view these recommendations from the Insights screen.

Also: Health is Tim Cook’s defining legacy – and your Apple Watch proves it.

Industry observers note that A latest feature called Health Age compares your physical health to your actual age to show how you’re doing. The analysis draws on certain stats and lab data, such as your resting heart rate, sleep, heart rate variability (HRV), cholesterol, and A1C (average blood glucose levels), to deliver a health age, which may differ from your chronological age. The results can show you areas that may be of concern or that you need to focus on.

Also: Apple Watch Series 12 review: Finally, the health tracker I’ve been waiting for.

In a recent development, with a new feature called Movement Evaluations and an iPhone and Apple Watch, the Health app can assess your flexibility, strength, balance, VO2 max (maximum oxygen absorption), and overall movement. You perform a physical routine while your iPhone “watches” you via the camera. Using built-in AI, the app will provide audio and visual feedback in real-time to tell you how you’re faring.

Apple promises that the analysis is performed on your device without recording, storing, or sharing the video.

According to recent reports, the latest app will be able to correlate your test results with data collected by your iPhone and Apple Watch to give you a more comprehensive picture of your health. Plus, Apple and Quest Diagnostics have teamed up to offer people in the US an optional $119 bloodwork panel that covers more than 50 biomarkers to scan for different health and medical conditions.

Also: I tested the Apple Watch Series 12 heart-rate claims against my gold-standard Polar strap.

Normally, you need an Apple Fitness+ subscription to fire up workout videos to help you exercise. But the latest Health app will come with its own comprehensive set of training videos. Available from the Insights section, a series of strength exercise videos are designed to help you build your body strength. The videos cover all the key areas of your body to give you a full workout.

Sources indicate that some of the fresh features, such as the strength videos, will be available to all iPhone consumers. But the ones that rely on AI will run only on phones that support Apple Intelligence. That means you’ll need an iPhone 15 Pro or Pro Max, any iPhone 16 or 17, an iPhone 18 Pro or Pro Max, an iPhone Air, or an iPhone Duo.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.
  • In a recent development, if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.

The rear display isn’t good for much, but these are great phones in almost every other respect.

In a recent development, if you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Xiaomi introduced a second screen to its flagship phones with last year’s 17 Pros, but didn’t release them outside China. That means the upcoming 18 Pro and Pro Max are the first chance I’ve had to find out if a screen on the back of a phone is any more useful now than it was when Xiaomi last tried it on 2021’s Mi 11 Ultra — not to mention earlier efforts by the likes of Nubia and Vivo.

After a week or two with both of Xiaomi’s new Pro phones, I’m not entirely sold. The rear display has a single, obvious use case — it’s helped me take some of the best selfies I’ve ever managed — but it isn’t very useful otherwise.

The rest of the phones are great, with good cameras, massive batteries, and a more flexible take on the privacy display seen in the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. There’s a lot to like. But with prices higher than ever thanks to the RAM crisis, it’s hard not to wonder how much buyers are paying for a second screen they could probably do without.

Excellent main and telephoto camerasPrivacy displayStrong performanceCompact.

Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive.

Excellent main and telephoto camerasPrivacy displayStrong performanceExtended dynamic range.

Rear display is limitedBasic ultrawide cameraExpensive.

There are two Xiaomi 18 Pro phones: the £1,199 Pro (around $1,570) and the £1,399 Pro Max (around $1,830). In the UK and Europe, they’re priced to compete directly with the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

According to recent reports, they come in similar sizes to the iPhones, too: a 6.4-inch display on the Pro, and 6.9 inches on the Pro Max. There are a few other differences, though not many. The Pro Max’s 7,050mAh battery is bigger than the Pro’s 6,000mAh (with larger batteries available outside Europe), and its 100W wired charging is 10W faster too. Both phones last a day pretty comfortably and will stretch to two with lighter use, though only just — I’ve seen better battery life from recent Oppo and Vivo flagships. They also use Qualcomm’s Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chips, though only the Pro Max has the Extreme version. And while the camera setups are nearly identical, you’ll get slightly better dynamic range from the bigger phone thanks to a LOFIC sensor.

It has been revealed that the rear screens also vary slightly in size between the phones, though at either 2.7 or 2.9 inches, there’s not much in it. Wrapping around the two main rear camera lenses, they look a lot like the displays you’ll find on the front of foldables like the Galaxy Z Flip 8, though smaller than most of those, and much more limited in functionality.

According to recent reports, you can set your choice of wallpapers, some of which are interactive. Listen to music or a podcast, and playback controls appear. You can turn on notifications, useful for when you want to rest your phone face down, but Xiaomi’s implementation is odd: App icons appear so large on the screen that there’s no space to fit much text from a given notification; there are no interactive responses like quick replies or marking emails as read; and you can’t see a list of your notifications, only viewing each for a few seconds as it comes in. It makes this just barely more useful than a notification LED.

Unlike flip phones, you can’t use the small screen to access the phone’s settings, and you certainly can’t run full-blown apps. Instead, there’s a natural-language AI tool to create your own apps, powered by Google’s Gemini 4 Argon. It’s good for simple tools or games — I made a pomodoro timer and a semi-functional knockoff Pac-Man — but your creations can’t connect to the internet or access other apps, so anything you make will be quite purposefully limited.

The only thing that’s convinced me the rear screen is at all worthwhile is its camera viewfinder. The UI’s a little fiddly at this scale, but you can take photos, record videos, or create a photo booth-inspired picture set, all using the rear main camera. I’ve taken the best selfies of my life with this phone, which may be reason enough for some people to buy it.

It helps that the main camera is especially good. It and the telephoto are both excellent 200-megapixel shooters with large sensors, capable of great results in almost any lighting conditions. The telephoto’s short minimum focusing distance of 12cm lets it double as a great macro camera too. The 18 Pro Max has a slight photographic advantage, with a LOFIC main sensor that offers an expanded 16-stop dynamic range, helping it capture better highlights in particularly tricky lighting. Most of the time you won’t see a huge difference between the two phones.

Xiaomi’s longtime camera partner Leica is involved again, and by default you can shoot in one of two Leica-branded camera modes — Vibrant or Authentic — plus a fresh third option, the Xiaomi-branded Original, which splits the difference between them. The other significant Leica contribution is a new Essential Moments mode that uses AI to simulate three different retro Leica aesthetics in either 35mm or 75mm lenses.

Sources indicate that the ultrawide, set apart from the other two lenses beneath the screen, looks like an afterthought — and it shoots like one too. It’s placed so low on the body that my finger frequently blocks its view; its 17mm focal length barely feels wider than the 23mm main camera, so it doesn’t give you much extra room to play with; and its smaller sensor means quality is noticeably worse than from either of the other rear cameras, especially in dimmer light. As for the selfie camera, it’s decent, but you’ll only ever use it for video calls since the rear screen makes the main camera the better choice the rest of the time.

It has been revealed that the Xiaomi 18 Pro phones have one other trick: a privacy display. This is a pretty direct imitation of Samsung’s Galaxy S26 Ultra tech, switching between different sets of pixels with varying viewing angles to make your screen hard to see from the side when it’s activated. Like Samsung’s version, you can turn it on across the phone or just for certain apps; unlike Samsung’s, when you activate it for specific apps, it also applies to specific notifications, and it works with split-screen or floating windows without affecting other apps open at the same time. It’s more flexible than Samsung’s version, though to my eye, less effective.

Recent findings suggest that the Xiaomi 18 Pro and Pro Max have plenty of strengths, with great main and telephoto cameras, good performance, and reasonably attractive designs. But shortcomings like the lackluster ultrawide camera and batteries that don’t last as long as some rival flagships make me wonder about the compromises made to fit that rear display. Its limited functionality has given me pause, especially as flagship phones like this hit increasingly eye-watering prices.

Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1002 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance.
  • Recent findings suggest that these devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers.
  • Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days. Now, Google is ready to take another swing at “intelligent eyewear” for the Gemini era after previewing its aims a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they’re no impulse buy.

Recent findings suggest that these devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered.

Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn’t told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.

Google claims the frames all weigh about 41 grams, which is not terrible but is definitely near the top for glasses generally. They will, naturally, weigh much more when you account for lenses. That will also determine the final pricing. So far, we only have the starting prices for these devices, including non-prescription lenses.

Sources indicate that the setup here is similar to the Ray-Ban Meta glasses we’ve seen for a few years. There are no screens in the lenses, but you can interact with the AI system via voice or by activating the integrated camera. The experience should be similar to using Gemini Live on your phone, but it will be a lot easier to fire up the AI. You can say “Hey Gemini” or tap a touch-sensitive area of the frame to start interacting with the robot.

Credit: Gentle Monster Credit: Gentle Monster.

Industry observers note that since this is the same chatbot that operates across the Google ecosystem, it has access to your data and preferences. You can ask questions and get personalized answers, have Google Maps guide you by voice, or just talk with the AI to kill time. The glasses use custom open-ear speakers to limit distractions for those around you. Google notes the directional microphones should not pick up speech from other people, either.

Adding the camera feed is where things get interesting. When the AI can see what you see, it has the potential to do more work on your behalf. Google suggests asking Gemini for recommendations when looking at a bookshelf or glancing at an event poster to have the AI add it to your calendar. The glasses will also support Gemini Guided Vision, which provides conversational audio descriptions for people who are visually impaired.

The utility of these devices hinges on Gemini. I would be remiss not to point out that Gemini, like all AI systems, is not infallible. In fact, it can be frustratingly fallible at times. The chatbot still regularly screws up simple things like adding calendar appointments or identifying objects in an image in my testing, and when you don’t have a screen to verify the AI’s output, it may be harder to trust it. These devices will really only make sense if you can rely on Gemini to do things right, and that’s still not a guarantee.

Sources indicate that all the Gemini-powered glasses from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker feature a 12 MP wide-angle camera capable of shooting photos and video. Google says it has implemented a number of features and limitations to ensure people don’t do creepy things with its intelligent eyewear, and that it doesn’t do creepy things to you—Google claims its approach respects privacy on “both sides of the lens.”.

For starters, there’s a recording light that is on whenever the camera is active. Like the Meta glasses, Google’s eyewear will detect if the light has been covered up or modified in any way that would prevent it from illuminating. In that event, the glasses will refuse to activate the camera. All Google-powered glasses will have a physical off switch, too.

Credit: Warby Parker Credit: Warby Parker.

In a recent development, on the user privacy side, Google says it will not save any images or videos captured by the glasses in your Gemini history. Additionally, none of that data will be used for training AI models or targeting ads. Your voice interactions with Gemini via the glasses are, as with all other Gemini endpoints, not guaranteed the same level of protection. You can delete your chats from the Gemini history, though.

Data on the glasses is encrypted, and it remains that way during transit to the cloud. However, it’s not encrypted on Google’s servers. The firm does note that it’s working to bring Private AI Compute to glasses, which will isolate data during processing so not even Google can access it.

Credit: Gentle Monster Credit: Gentle Monster.

Anyone looking to get Gemini on their face and test Google’s privacy promise can preorder the glasses from the Gentle Monster and Warby Parker websites. Devices should ship and appear on store shelves on December 10. Importantly, support for these devices is a bit narrow at launch. They will work with all iPhones from the 13 Pro onward. On the Android side, you’ll need a Pixel 7 or newer or a Samsung Galaxy S or Z series device running One UI 9 or later. If you’ve got a cheaper Samsung Galaxy or a device from another OEM, you’re out of luck at the moment.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Google Wallet app is available for iPhone consumers in the US for the first time.
  • Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits.
  • In a recent development, the new Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Google Wallet app is available for iPhone consumers in the US for the first time. iOS users who download the fresh Google Wallet app can manage online payments for faster checkout at places that support Google Pay. However, Apple restricts Google’s ability to offer tap-to-pay service on the iOS app, so users won’t be able to use Google Wallet for contactless checkout on iPhone.

Also: You can use Google’s Spark AI agent, renamed Tasks, for free now – with limits.

In a recent development, the new Google Wallet app lets you digitize physical cards, including payment, loyalty, and membership cards, as well as boarding passes. Google Wallet app owners on iOS will also be able to view receipts and track orders pulled from Gmail in one app.

According to recent reports, there used to be a Google Pay app for iOS, but it was discontinued in 2024. The old Google Pay app also didn’t support tap-to-pay on iPhone, but it offered limited functionality, including support for loyalty and gift cards, as well as purchase tracking.

The biggest difference between the old Google Pay app for iOS and the upcoming Google Wallet is the AI component, which supports agentic shopping, likely as Google’s longer-term play.

One of Google’s goals for the Wallet app on iOS is to make it a central place to manage purchases made by its AI agents. The Agents section in Google Wallet for iPhone lets you manage and monitor purchases made through Gemini.

Sources indicate that agentic commerce is on the rise, as evidenced by the growing use of Meta’s Muse. Gemini can make purchases and payments through the Tasks feature, which lets you give Gemini permission to buy the items you want and set your maximum budget.

Also: Google Wallet just turned your Android phone into a digital house key.

The Google Wallet app for iOS becomes the central hub for purchase management in agentic commerce through Gemini. In it, you can view active tasks to see which purchases Gemini is working on, as well as completed purchases and receipts.

Google has been working on two technologies to support its agentic commerce strategy: Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP) and Agent Payments Protocol (AP2).

UCP is a technical language that enables AI agents to communicate with retailers and make purchases, while AP2 is the payment framework that establishes rules and authorization for agents to make payments.

Google Wallet serves as both the AI-powered wallet and the consumer-facing record of transactions made by Gemini.

Also: Google Wallet has a lot of new tricks – these 5 are my favorites.

Recent findings suggest that along with Google, major retailers supported the development of UCP, including Shopify, Walmart, Target, and Etsy. When Google revealed AP2, more than 60 organizations became involved, including PayPal, Salesforce, Mastercard, and American Express.
